new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Bow 1997, A description of Moloko phonology, (image-only, 42 pp.). Rendered PDF page 6 (printed p. 5) myself and read it: footnote 5 reads exactly 'In Moloko stress falls on the final syllable in a phrase, which always has a heavy syllable.' The same passage is in the scanned at line 301. Sec. 2.1.2 defines heavy as containing a +Low (full) vowel, following Goldsmith's full-vs-reduced distinction, and p. 6 (PDF 7) says 'In word-final position, before a pause, the final syllable, whether open or closed, must be a heavy syllable'; sec. 2.3.4 (PDF 12) repeats that citation forms show the pre-pausal final syllable as heavy while in context the final vowel is -Low. No word-level stress rule; ton…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (Friesen 2017, A grammar of Moloko, pp. 38-39, 64, 179: 'the final syllable before a pause is stressed', 'stress is phrase-final'; catalog classification PHRASAL, domain phrase). Bow 1997 is the source Friesen 2017 cites for the phonology, and it states the same pre-pausal/phrase-final stress with the same full-vowel correlate. Chapter 4 (pp. 36-40) describes the tone system (two underlying tones H/L, three surface tones via depressor consonants) separately from stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is stated at the phrase level: the final syllable of a phrase is stressed, and that syllable is always heavy, where Bow defines heavy as containing a full (+Low) vowel rather than by CVC/CVV; the same page says the vowel in word-final pre-pausal position must be +Low. No word-level stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated in the footnote; the main text notes that in word-final pre-pausal position the syllable must be heavy (full vowel), which is the correlate of the phrase-final stress. Bow's 'heavy' is full versus reduced vowel, not syllable shape.
new_statements.identity_note: Bow 1997 (p. 1) reports that a 1996 SIL sociolinguistic survey found no distinctive dialects of Moloko, only village-level accent differences with full intercomprehension; her sketch is based on two speakers, one from Mbidémé (foot of Moloko Mountain) and one from the Ftak clan raised in Gayak Assideo. Works 2 and 3 are the same document (the 2004 SIL Cameroon version of Friesen & Mamalis, The Moloko verb phrase), and work 1 is its 2008 SIL EWP revision, so the four listed entries are really two distinct works.
